The Stratospheric Controlled Perturbation Experiment (SCoPEx) was a Harvard University scientific proposal to study how tiny amounts of aerosol particles behave in the stratosphere. Principal investigator Frank Keutsch and collaborators including David Keith described the concept publicly, including at the American Geophysical Union Fall Meeting in 2017. The experiment was designed to improve computer models used to estimate risks and benefits of solar geoengineering (solar radiation management). It was not a test of deploying geoengineering and was not intended to cool the planet. The planned platform was a scientific balloon gondola with propellers, flying near 20 km altitude. A very small amount of material — on the order of 100 grams to less than 2 kilograms, typically calcium carbonate (a common mineral found in limestone and used in products such as toothpaste) — would be released into a small mixed volume roughly 1 km long and 100 meters in diameter. The gondola would then fly back through that plume to measure aerosol microphysics, chemistry, and light scattering. A 2021 platform test in Sweden, planned with the Swedish Space Corporation from Esrange, was a hardware test only: the SCoPEx Advisory Committee recommended suspending it pending societal engagement, and no particles were to be released. In March 2024 Harvard announced that Keutsch was no longer pursuing SCoPEx; the platform is expected to be repurposed for stratospheric research unrelated to solar geoengineering.

Achieving the goals of the Paris Agreement necessitates substantial and sustained reductions in fossil CO2, methane, and other greenhouse gases, alongside the preservation of carbon sinks.

(2013, 2016) and related studies of peer-reviewed abstracts found that among papers taking a position, about 97% endorsed anthropogenic global warming; later surveys of publishing climate scientists find similarly high agreement. Claims that 'there is no consensus' or that a petition of non-climate specialists overturns IPCC assessments misrepresent how scientific agreement is established. A 2019 'European Climate Declaration' signed by hundreds of people, including many without climate-research credentials, does not negate the assessed literature. Uncertainty remains about the exact magnitude of climate sensitivity and regional impacts, not about whether adding CO2 warms the planet.
